Is the Four-Day Work Week Ready for Canada?

Last year, a mid-sized software company in Halifax made headlines when it moved its 120 employees to a four-day week with no reduction in pay. Twelve months later, the company reports that productivity has stayed the same, while sick days have fallen by nearly a third. Its chief executive, Maria Chen, says the change has also made hiring easier. “We used to lose candidates to bigger firms in Toronto,” she explains. “Now people apply to us because of the schedule.”

Supporters argue that a shorter week allows employees to rest, spend time with their families, and return to work more focused. They point to trials in the United Kingdom and Iceland, where most participating companies chose to keep the shorter schedule after the experiment ended. Some economists also believe a four-day week could reduce traffic and lower energy use in office buildings.

Critics, however, warn that the model does not suit every industry. Hospitals, schools, and retail stores need staff to be present every day, and moving to four days often means hiring more workers or asking current staff to work longer shifts. Small business owners worry about the cost. “For a restaurant like mine, a fifth day of wages has to come from somewhere,” says Tom Bergeron, who owns a bistro in Quebec City. “Usually it comes from customers through higher prices.”

Others suggest a middle path. Instead of a strict four-day schedule, they recommend giving employees more control over when they work, such as compressed hours or flexible start times. According to labour researcher Dr. Aisha Rahman, flexibility matters more to workers than the number of days. “What people really want,” she says, “is the ability to plan their work around their lives, not the other way around.”
